pack.description: Vocabulary of economics and business passages and talks: markets, policy, firms and trade.
pack.selection_note: Internal selection of terms that recur in introductory economics texts; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: a general rise in prices over time, so that money buys less
entries.example_academic: High inflation erodes the real value of savings.
entries.example_spoken: With this inflation, my rent goes up every year.

entries.definition: money that a government pays to make a product or service cheaper or to support an industry
entries.example_academic: Agricultural subsidies keep domestic prices above world levels.
entries.example_spoken: The bus pass is cheap because of a city subsidy.

entries.definition: a tax that a government charges on goods coming into the country
entries.example_academic: The tariff on imported steel raised costs for domestic car makers.
entries.example_spoken: Prices went up after the new tariff came in.

entries.definition: a basic product, such as oil, wheat or copper, that is bought and sold in large quantities
entries.example_academic: Countries that export a single commodity are exposed to sudden price changes.
entries.example_spoken: Coffee is the most traded commodity after oil, apparently.

entries.definition: a situation in which one company controls the whole supply of a product or service
entries.example_academic: The railway held a monopoly on freight and set prices accordingly.
entries.example_spoken: The campus bookstore basically has a monopoly on textbooks.

entries.definition: something that encourages a person to do something
entries.example_academic: Tax incentives encouraged firms to invest in research.
entries.example_spoken: There's no incentive to finish early if you don't get paid more.

entries.definition: the money that a company or government receives from sales or taxes
entries.example_academic: Advertising accounts for most of the platform's revenue.
entries.example_spoken: The café's revenue doubled when it started opening on Sundays.

entries.definition: the amount by which money spent is greater than money received
entries.example_academic: The government financed the deficit by borrowing from abroad.
entries.example_spoken: The club ended the year with a small deficit.

entries.definition: a period when the economy of a country shrinks and there is less business activity
entries.example_academic: Unemployment continued to rise for a year after the recession officially ended.
entries.example_spoken: She graduated in the middle of a recession.

entries.definition: a situation in which there is not enough of something that people need or want
entries.example_academic: Economics begins from the scarcity of resources relative to human wants.
entries.example_spoken: There's a scarcity of affordable housing near campus.

entries.definition: relating to government taxes and spending
entries.example_academic: Fiscal policy was loosened in order to stimulate demand.
entries.example_spoken: The university's fiscal year ends in June.

entries.definition: relating to money, especially the amount of money in an economy
entries.example_academic: The central bank tightened monetary policy to slow rising prices.
entries.example_spoken: The prize has more symbolic than monetary value.

entries.definition: the rate at which goods or services are produced, especially for each worker or hour
entries.example_academic: Gains in productivity allowed wages to rise without increasing prices.
entries.example_spoken: My productivity drops to zero after lunch.

entries.definition: the act of using goods, energy or food, or the amount that is used
entries.example_academic: Household consumption fell sharply as interest rates climbed.
entries.example_spoken: We're trying to cut our energy consumption this winter.

entries.definition: a person who starts a business and takes financial risks in order to make money
entries.example_academic: Entrepreneurs respond to gaps that established firms have overlooked.
entries.example_spoken: My roommate sees herself as a future entrepreneur.

entries.definition: the value of the best thing you give up when you choose to do something else
entries.example_academic: The opportunity cost of attending university includes the wages a student could have earned.
entries.example_spoken: The opportunity cost of this meeting is two hours of studying.

entries.definition: a measure of how much the amount people buy or sell changes when the price changes
entries.example_academic: The elasticity of demand for fuel is low because drivers have few alternatives.
entries.example_spoken: If demand has low elasticity, raising the price barely changes sales.

entries.definition: an effect of an economic activity on people who are not directly involved in it and do not pay for or get paid for it
entries.example_academic: Pollution is a negative externality that the market price of the product ignores.
entries.example_spoken: Noise from the stadium is an externality for the neighbors.

entries.definition: a market that is controlled by a small number of large companies
entries.example_academic: In an oligopoly, each firm must anticipate the reactions of its few rivals.
entries.example_spoken: The phone market is an oligopoly: three companies and that's it.

entries.definition: a government policy of spending less and taxing more in order to reduce debt
entries.example_academic: Austerity reduced the deficit but deepened the recession in the short term.
entries.example_spoken: After years of austerity, the library had almost no staff left.

entries.definition: the state of having money that is available at once, or of being easy to turn into cash
entries.example_academic: Banks hoarded liquidity because they doubted the solvency of their partners.
entries.example_spoken: The company has assets but no liquidity to pay salaries.

entries.definition: a fall in the value of something over time
entries.example_academic: The depreciation of the currency made exports cheaper abroad.
entries.example_spoken: A new car loses a lot to depreciation in the first year.

entries.definition: the policy of helping a country's own industries by taxing or limiting goods from other countries
entries.example_academic: Protectionism shields domestic producers at the expense of consumers.
entries.example_spoken: The article argues that protectionism always backfires.

entries.definition: the ability of a country or person to produce something at a lower cost, in terms of other goods given up, than others can
entries.example_academic: Trade benefits both partners when each specializes according to its comparative advantage.
entries.example_spoken: Our team has a comparative advantage in design, so let's focus on that.

entries.definition: the situation in which each extra unit of effort or money produces a smaller extra result than the one before
entries.example_academic: Adding more workers to the same machine soon leads to diminishing returns.
entries.example_spoken: After midnight, studying gives you diminishing returns.

entries.definition: a state of balance, for example when the amount supplied equals the amount demanded
entries.example_academic: The market reaches equilibrium at the price where supply matches demand.
entries.example_spoken: It took the housing market years to get back to equilibrium.

entries.definition: property that a borrower promises to give to a lender if the loan is not paid back
entries.example_academic: Small farmers were refused credit because they could offer no collateral.
entries.example_spoken: He put up his house as collateral for the loan.

entries.definition: the removal of government rules and controls from an industry
entries.example_academic: Deregulation of the airline industry lowered fares but reduced service to small towns.
entries.example_spoken: Prices dropped after deregulation, at least for a while.

entries.definition: the risk that people behave less carefully when they know someone else will pay for their mistakes
entries.example_academic: Guaranteeing every bank deposit creates moral hazard, since lenders stop watching risk.
entries.example_spoken: If insurance covers everything, there's a moral hazard: people stop being careful.

entries.definition: based on guessing rather than knowledge; or done in the hope of quick profit despite high risk
entries.example_academic: Speculative buying pushed house prices far above their long-term trend.
entries.example_spoken: That's a bit speculative; do you have any data?
